bibliographic.title: Leaving Goals on the Pitch: Evaluating Decision Making in Soccer
bibliographic.venue: MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference 2021 (Soccer Track AMVC3NU3A)

scope.rationale: Paper proposes a Markov Decision Process framework learned from event-stream data to evaluate team shooting policies via counterfactual reasoning (probabilistic model checking), assigning location-based shot values and analyzing decision making (shoot vs. move). Directly relevant to action valuation and decision recommendation for shots.

model.name: MDP-based counterfactual shooting-decision framework (Van Roy et al. 2021)
inputs: ball location (state defined by current location of the ball)
field partitioned into a 22-by-17 grid over the offensive half plus a single state for the defensive half (375 field states)
three absorbing states: s_goal, s_no_goal, s_loss_possession
event-stream data of passes, dribbles and shots (StatsBomb)
characteristics of actions and what happened prior to the actions (used by GBDT to predict intended end location of actions)
StatsBomb xG values for individual shots (used to approximate the frequency-vs-efficiency trade-off)
model.target: Per-team MDP comprising: P(s, move_to(s'), s') (probability of successfully moving the ball from s to s'), P(s, shoot, s_goal) (location-based xG, i.e., probability of scoring from s), and policy pi(a|s); used to compute E[goals | pi] = sum_s E[shots in s | pi] * P(s, shoot, s_goal).
model.architecture: Closed-form Markov Decision Process learned per team from event data; Gradient Boosted Trees Ensembles used to predict intended end locations of move actions (to estimate transition probabilities); PRISM probabilistic model checker used to compute properties (e.g., probability of generating a better shot later) and STORM mentioned as an alternative; counterfactual policy alteration via proportional re-weighting of action probabilities; expected number of state visits computed from the MDP fundamental matrix N = (I - Q)^-1.
model.spatial_resolution: 22-by-17 grid over the offensive half (3.1m x 3.1m cells) plus a single state for the defensive half; 375 field states in total
model.temporal_horizon: until possession ends (absorbing states s_goal, s_no_goal, s_loss_possession); also aggregated to a full season via expected number of state visits

metrics: average relative error between estimated and actual number of goals per team (11.38%)
expected number of goals per season under a policy (E[goals | pi])
difference in xG between move-then-shoot scenarios and shooting immediately
probability of ever generating a better shot than the current one within the same possession
evaluation.splits: Per-team MDPs learned from 17 teams that appeared in both the 2017/18 and 2018/19 EPL seasons (76 matches per team); no explicit train/test split reported. Accuracy assessed by comparing estimated number of goals scored (under the observed policy) to actual goals recorded in the data for each team.

claims.statement: The seven high-volume long-distance shooters (Eriksen, Pogba, Kane, De Bruyne, Son, Hazard, Sigurdsson) converted 6.5% of their 416 long-distance shots across the 2017/18 and 2018/19 EPL; in the 4455 times these seven players touched the ball in the long-distance zone and did not shoot, their teams only ended up scoring a goal in 2.1% of these possessions.
The MDP partitions the offensive half of the pitch into a 22-by-17 grid and uses a single state for the defensive half, yielding 375 field states (cells are 3.1m x 3.1m).
The MDPs are learned per team using StatsBomb event stream data from the 2017/18 and 2018/19 English Premier League, considering only the 17 teams that appeared in both seasons (76 matches per team).

The average relative error between the estimated number of goals scored according to the observed-policy analysis and the actual number of goals recorded for each team is 11.38%; for an average team scoring around 50 goals per season this corresponds to roughly six goals.
claims.evidence_location: Section 3.2.2 (Accuracy of estimating the number of goals), page 10

claims.statement: The probability of ever generating a better shot in the same possession can be as low as 5% in some locations; on the edge of the box directly in front of goal it is only between 5% and 10%; in other locations (e.g., Manchester United's left side of attack) it can be around 20%.

Uniformly increasing the frequency of long-distance shooting by 5%, 10%, or 20% increases the expected number of goals per season for most teams (e.g., Chelsea +0.3 / +0.5 / +1.0; Everton +0.2 / +0.4 / +0.8); some teams (Burnley, Liverpool, Newcastle United) see no gains or a slight decrease.

A targeted increase in long-distance shooting (only from locations where shooting was deemed better than moving) yields expected-goal gains for all teams: shooting 10% more often yields about an additional half a goal per season, and 20% more often yields roughly an extra goal for most teams (e.g., Chelsea +1.6 at +20%).
Per-team analysis identifies specific long-distance zones where increasing shot frequency by 10-20% would likely lead to an increase of 0.5-1.5 goals in a season.

Using data from the last ten EPL seasons (2010/11 to 2019/20), the figure shows that every goal scored during a season equates to roughly one point in the final table (fit Points = 0.956 x Goals scored + 2.451).

limitations: The 6.5% conversion figure for the seven long-distance shooters is likely an underestimate as rebounds (i.e., other chances created due to a shot from distance) are not taken into account (footnote 1, page 2).

Event stream data records the location where the ball went out of bounds but not the location it was intended to reach; hence the number of unsuccessful move actions from state s intended to reach state s' cannot be directly estimated from data and must be approximated using a Gradient Boosted Trees Ensemble (Section 2.2, page 6).
The MDP uses a coarse partitioning (22-by-17 in the offensive half, single state for the defensive half) chosen as a trade-off between expressiveness and data sparsity (Section 2.1, page 4).

Accurately modeling the frequency-versus-efficiency trade-off when altering the policy would be a complicated undertaking in its own right; the paper approximates it with a simpler adjustment based on the StatsBomb xG distribution within each state (Section 3.2.2, 'Estimating P'(s, shoot, s_goal) in pi'', pages 9-10).
open_questions: Extend the framework to other aspects of the game, e.g., analyzing whether a forward or a backward throw-in is more suitable in a specific situation, and how to effectively play out from the back (Section 6, Conclusions).
Further investigate the full potential of the framework (Section 6, Conclusions).
